toc.title: Safety isn't supposed to be on all the time

sections.title: Look, listen, then let yourself feel wonder
Feel it in your real body

toc.title: When flight or fight energy shows up

blocks.p: A few things came up in a conversation with members of one of my courses that I think are really worth sharing. The first is pendulation, and how it can happen naturally in grieving, which is something I see in therapy a lot. The second is whether the safety state needs to be on at all times, and whether that's even the goal of all this polyvagal stuff. The third is using your imagination as a safety anchor. And at the end, one member shares how her triggers have softened as she's built her safety anchors.
One member put it this way: trying to be mindful without first grounding her senses and having that safety present was very uncomfortable.

She's totally right. Trying to be mindful of what's happening within you before you're anchored in safety can be really difficult and scary. That is not easy to do, to feel your dysregulation. I think you have to be anchored in your safety state first. Otherwise, I don't think it'd be very helpful. It might even be re-traumatizing.

Pendulation is tapping into a dysregulated state a little bit, and then swaying back to safety. A lot of people do this on a regular basis, naturally, but without a lot of mindfulness. And sometimes, as that same member described, the swing gets too big, and you land in one state and can't swing yourself back.

I can definitely see that happening with people if they don't have familiarity with their safety state and don't know how to access it. It could pendulate one way and then not be able to swing back. And then you kind of have to wait for it to run its course. If you send yourself into a panic attack, you have to wait for it to finish, and then eventually come back.

I think there's a natural capacity to pendulate, and I notice it a lot with my clients who are grieving. They've lost someone, and there seems to be this natural capacity to be sad and angry and in the grieving process.

If someone can be with that, I notice they'll just naturally, spontaneously remember something about that person that brings them happiness. Their safety state comes on, and then story follows state: they remember something positive and can share it out loud.

So there's this natural capacity to grieve, in deep sadness and anger and mourning, and also to balance it out with "ah, but there was this one time that this person did this thing," and to smile. To reflect on that, and then come back to sadness and all the other mourning and grieving feelings. Then back to appreciation, and building new meaning for their life. That's where I see it in therapy most recognizably: when someone is grieving and really feeling their feelings, they'll pendulate naturally on their own.

One member, who was taking time off after an injury, recognized this in herself. She said there was a lot of grief and anger: why did this happen to me, is this my own fault, a lot of story follows state. She said she was literally feeling into her shutdown a lot. And then she could come back, sometimes quickly, other times it took a little more. She could appreciate the things she was learning through the experience, the relationships that keep her going, and reprioritizing her life. Those were the thoughts that follow a state of more safety.

It can happen naturally. It's great to recognize it, even if it's after it happens. But while it's happening, we might be able to notice it and really experience it, and bring a little more mindfulness, or awareness, to the natural process.

blocks.h: Safety isn't supposed to be on all the time

blocks.p: It's important to normalize this. It's not possible to be 100% in your safety state all the time, and I don't even know if that's the goal of all this. I kind of don't think it is. We want to be able to access it.

I think that if we're growing as individuals, dysregulation is part of that. If we're always in our safety state, what does that say about our growth potential? Doesn't that mean we're just kind of always happy or something? I can't imagine what that life would be like, and I don't know if I even want that. That would mean there's no more possibility for growth. You'd have to be pretty cut off, or extremely accepting and empathetic and unendingly positive, and I don't think that's possible.

I wasn't even thinking about what's coming at us throughout the day. I was thinking about our potential for growth. If we're always challenging ourselves, there's always going to be some dysregulation. We're going to go from our safety state down to flight or fight when we have new things in life that are different, obstacles we have to overcome. That might be interviewing for a new job, or applying for one, or admitting you're ready for a new job. It could be exiting a relationship. It could be small or big life milestones that are challenges. How can you stay 100% in your safety state through those? Don't you kind of have to drop down and be in some flight or fight, or maybe even shutdown?
We just want to have access to safety. We don't want to lose access to it. We want to stay anchored in it.

Another member added that the people she knows who claim to always be in a positive state seem to her to be in denial, and that the whole idea of feeling your feelings would cause some dysregulation, some discomfort.
Dr. Porges said it this way on the podcast:

q: Safety is not a constant state. Safety is part of a range of engagement, disengagement, and re-engagement.
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [From Sound to Safety: Understanding the Safe & Sound Protocol with Dr. Porges and Karen Onderko (episode 254)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/20b541da-11ef-4b2e-b911-42b6ceba2bd1)

blocks.p: One of the safety anchors I teach is imagination. One member was struggling with it. As a child, with a lot going on around her in her family, she used imagination to cope. She'd always come up with stories to tell herself. It was a good coping strategy in one way, but it had a flight flavor to it: escaping into an alternate reality. She's an artist, and she loves making up worlds with a storyline. But she wondered whether going into a world she created, instead of the environment she's actually in, is grounding at all.

I differentiate avoidance and escape. When we're not trying to feel our feelings, that's avoiding them. Escape is more when you're feeling your flight energy and you're utilizing it, and you get that release, and you can actually climb your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system).

If you're using your thoughts to avoid what you're feeling, that's entertainment, that's distraction. And that's not bad. That's totally fine, especially in a crisis moment. But building safety anchors isn't about avoiding your feelings. It's about creating safety.

Each of these ideas might not be a good fit for everybody. Movement might be a really big struggle for one person, whereas using their imagination is exactly right for them. These are just ideas. Among the cognitive anchors, maybe imagination isn't a good fit for you, or maybe it's meant something else to you. If so, it might be a big obstacle, and you can rely on one of the other cognitive anchors instead.

blocks.h3: Look, listen, then let yourself feel wonder

blocks.p: When it comes to using your imagination, I love Studio Ghibli movies, and they're a good example. The point is not to get lost in the story and escape your problems. The point is to look at the colors, look at the images, maybe hear the voices. That's one step: just sensory input.

The next step could be to allow yourself to feel wonder and awe and excitement. Imagination can bring those experiences to us. So it's not avoidance or entertainment. That's not what we're going for. We're going for experiencing a different world, potentially.
Using your imagination can also mean creating a safe space. Put generally: where would you go to feel safe? That's kind of a big question, so narrow it down:

ul: Where would you go to feel playfulness?
Where would you go to feel wonder?
Where would you go to feel creativity?

blocks.p: That might create a specific image. Maybe one of those words is the one you latch onto: "To feel creative, I would go to Main Street in Disneyland with a canvas and paint." That would be my place to feel safe, but specifically to feel creative.

So imagination doesn't have to be given to you through a movie. You can create it, and focus on what aspect of safety you want to feel. That could be creativity, playfulness, fun, curiosity, solitude, wonder.

blocks.h3: Feel it in your real body

blocks.p: When you use your imagination and feel those feelings, ask: are you feeling it in your real body, in the moment, in the room? Or are you imagining what it would be like to feel it, so that the imaginary version of you in that scenario is feeling it, and you're just remembering or thinking about how it would feel?

When you watch Studio Ghibli, or when you create a scenario, ask: how does this feel in my real body right now, when I use my mind to create this situation? Is it bringing more safety? Not just "can I create a character that feels safety," but "can I, in my real body, feel safety?"

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: When flight or fight energy shows up

blocks.p: That member created what she calls her play world, an imaginary world about the clouds, very playful and wonderful. Along with wonder and fun and curiosity and creativity, she sometimes felt some flighty energy, something exhilarated, and she wondered if that was bad, if she should be feeling more safety instead.

It's not bad. Not at all. It's just a feeling. None of these things are good or bad. They might feel more positive or more negative, and that's how we classify them, but they have no inherent worth. Nature doesn't assign good or bad feelings. They're just feelings, and they come from impulses our body has not been able to act on. So having flight activation is not bad. If you use your imagination and other feelings come in, as you're ready, let yourself have them and experience them.

It's actually very possible that you're accessing enough safety that you're allowing your body to start climbing its ladder. If you're activating the safety state enough, some other defensive stuff may come along with it. That's okay too.

As far as building safety anchors goes, I wouldn't encourage you to delve deeper into that activation. Noticing it is fine. Being curious about it is fine. But prioritize this: can I feel this, and also stay in my safety state? That's the priority. Delving deeper into what's coming up comes later. For now, notice it, let it be there, and prioritize anchoring.

One member shared how her anchors have changed her reactions. She was looking at some videos on TRE ahead of a class, and because the exercises are physical, the thought of them made her think, "This is going to trigger me." She immediately reminded herself: "Wait a minute. You're in your home. You're safe. Nobody else is around you."
She described it this way:

q: It feels to me like with some of these ways that I'm anchoring myself, I'm able to not have to be in the experience for very long before I recognize what anchors work for me. When I'm walking and joggers come up from behind me, I used to startle, and I could feel the adrenaline flowing, and my whole body would be in it for hours. To a degree it still is, but not as intense. Now when it happens, I can access my anger about it, not at them, but at what happened, and access my safety anchors: do my reality check, look around at the trees, feel the breeze, remember I'm going on a walk. Most times, not always, it's so integrated now that I don't have to be in the experience for such a long time and keep repeating it in my thoughts.

blocks.p: She does this work in her own therapy too, but having a list of choices gave it a baseline. She knows music doesn't work for her. She knows certain things that work in general. But each situation is different, so she goes down the list to see what works, and keeps going until she feels her brain is back online.

That's what we're going for. She's able to notice what's happening within her when she drops down the ladder, and regulate her way out of it, or at least enough to get back to a baseline she's happy with.
